---
title: "What Drives Ground-Level Ozone in Aotizhongxin, Beijing?"
author: "Sidrah Nawaz"
date: "2026-07-13"
output:
  pdf_document: default
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, dpi = 150, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)


for (packages in c("tidyverse", "lubridate", "skimr", "corrplot", "glmnet", "leaps", "boot")) {
  if (!require(packages, character.only = TRUE)) install.packages(packages) }

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(skimr)
library(corrplot)
library(glmnet)     # for Ridge and Lasso
library(boot)       # for cv.glm

```




We are using the 'Aotizhongxin' station dataset for now, think about expanding to other datasets if time!!

```{r step1}
# Read the CSV
air <- read.csv("PRSA_Data_Aotizhongxin_20130301-20170228.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Quick peek into data, everything checks out
glimpse(air)
dim(air)
```



O3 has 1,719 missing values. Since O3 is the target variable, let's remove them rather than impute

```{r step2}
# Check total missing values
sum(is.na(air %>%
  select(O3, TEMP, RAIN, WSPM, PRES, DEWP)))

# Check statistics before cleaned data
summary(air %>%
  select(O3, TEMP, RAIN, WSPM, PRES, DEWP))

# Check for duplicates
sum(duplicated(air))

```

       
       
       


```{r step3}

# Take out O3 rows
air_clean <- air %>% filter(!is.na(O3))

# Mean imputation of N/A feature variable rows
air_clean <- air_clean %>%
  mutate(
    TEMP = ifelse(is.na(TEMP), mean(TEMP, na.rm = TRUE), TEMP),
    PRES = ifelse(is.na(PRES), mean(PRES, na.rm = TRUE), PRES),
    RAIN = ifelse(is.na(RAIN), mean(RAIN, na.rm = TRUE), RAIN),
    WSPM = ifelse(is.na(WSPM), mean(WSPM, na.rm = TRUE), WSPM),
    DEWP = ifelse(is.na(DEWP), mean(DEWP, na.rm = TRUE), DEWP)
  )

# Summary statistics after cleaning
summary(air_clean %>%
  select(O3, TEMP, RAIN, WSPM, PRES, DEWP))
```




```{r step4}

# Select only the weather variables and O3 from the cleaned dataset
model_data <- air_clean %>%
  select(O3, TEMP, PRES, RAIN, WSPM, DEWP)  # These are the numerical weather factors, technically wd is a potential factor as well but I didn't include that!


# Pairwise scatterplots, storing it as an image to decrease file size
png(
  "pairs_plot.png",
  width = 6,
  height = 4,
  units = "in",
  res = 1800
)

pairs(model_data, col = "steelblue", main = "Weather vs Ozone")
invisible(dev.off())


# Correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- cor(model_data, use = "complete.obs")
corrplot(cor_matrix, method = "number", type = "upper", tl.cex = 0.8)
```

```{r pairs_image, echo=FALSE, out.width="99%", fig.align='center'}
#output of pairs plot for optimal sizing
knitr::include_graphics("pairs_plot.png")
```

From the pairwise scatterplot shown above, I can visually see there is a positive correlation between O3 and TEMP, and O3 and DEWP. O3 and RAIN is kind of weird..., sort of like a negative correlation. O3 and PRES has a clear negative correlation. O3 and WSPM has somewhat of a negative correlation.

Okay odd... Now the actual correlations say O3 and TEMP, WSPM, and DEWP have a positive correlation, O3 and RAIN is almost like 0 lol which is pretty accurate, and O3 and PRES has a negative correlation.

Very interesting! I have apparently encountered the "Simpson's paradox," as I thought WSPM was negative, but it's actually a positive correlation!





Since this is a time series, we need to split based of: Train on the PAST, test on the FUTURE. It's kind of like cheating if we train on the future and test in the past since the factors would already have been determined for what impacts the Ozone
```{r step5}

# Train/Test Split by Year (like the Smarket split thingy)
train_idx <- air_clean$year < 2016
test_idx <- !train_idx

x_train <- model_data[train_idx, ] %>% select(-O3)
y_train <- model_data[train_idx, ]$O3
x_test <- model_data[test_idx, ] %>% select(-O3)
y_test <- model_data[test_idx, ]$O3

# Check sizes
dim(x_train)
dim(x_test)
```
Test size is significantly bigger than train... is that okay? No! split at a greater year, not 2014! Okay we can test on 2016 instead, and that's lowk okay because it's an around 70% to 30% split, which is MUCH better than a 20% to 80% split!!!






```{r step6}
lm_fit <- lm(O3 ~ ., data = model_data[train_idx, ])
summary(lm_fit)
```





```{r step7}
# Diagnostic plots - like Ch 3 lab
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(lm_fit)

# Studentized residuals - outliers
rstudent_values <- rstudent(lm_fit)
outliers <- which(abs(rstudent_values) > 3)
cat("\nOutliers:", length(outliers), "\n")

# Leverage statistics - high leverage points
leverage_values <- hatvalues(lm_fit)
p <- 5
n <- nrow(air_clean)
leverage_threshold <- 2 * (p + 1) / n
high_leverage <- which(leverage_values > leverage_threshold)
cat("High-leverage points:", length(high_leverage), "\n")

# Cook's distance - influential observations
cooks_values <- cooks.distance(lm_fit)
cooks_threshold <- 4 / n
influential <- which(cooks_values > cooks_threshold)
cat("Influential points:", length(influential), "\n")
```






```{r step8}
# Prepare matrix
x_train_mat <- as.matrix(x_train)
x_test_mat <- as.matrix(x_test)

# Grid of lambda values
grid <- 10^seq(10, -2, length = 100)

# Ridge
ridge_cv <- cv.glmnet(x_train_mat, y_train, alpha = 0, lambda = grid)
best_ridge_lambda <- ridge_cv$lambda.min

# Extract coefficients at best lambda
ridge_coef <- coef(ridge_cv, s = best_ridge_lambda)
ridge_coef
```
I don't understand the Ridge Regression method AS MUCH as Lasso, but interestingly we're getting very very similar numeric results for both methods! This means (I think) that the model is already really stable, so there doesn't have to be extreme changes to the coefficients. But then that kind of means these methods are not as significant/necessary, and linear modeling is perfectly fine.





```{r step9}
# Fit Lasso with cross-validation
set.seed(1)
lasso_cv <- cv.glmnet(x_train_mat, y_train, alpha = 1, lambda = grid)

# Plot the cross-validation error
plot(lasso_cv, main = "Lasso Cross-Validation Error")

# Find the best lambda
best_lasso_lambda <- lasso_cv$lambda.min
best_lasso_lambda

# Extract coefficients at the optimal penalty
lasso_coef <- coef(lasso_cv, s = best_lasso_lambda)
lasso_coef
```






```{r step10}
lasso_full <- glmnet(x_train_mat, y_train, alpha = 1, lambda = grid)
plot(lasso_full, xvar = "lambda", label = TRUE, main = "Lasso Coefficient Path")
# This plot shows variables dropping to zero as lambda increases.
```


```{r step11}

# Predict on test set using Linear Regression
linear_pred <- predict(lm_fit, newdata = x_test)
linear_test_mse <- mean((linear_pred - y_test)^2)

# Predict on test set using Ridge
ridge_pred <- predict(ridge_cv, newx = x_test_mat, s = best_ridge_lambda)
ridge_test_mse <- mean((ridge_pred - y_test)^2)

# Predict on test set using Lasso
lasso_pred <- predict(lasso_cv, newx = x_test_mat, s = best_lasso_lambda)
lasso_test_mse <- mean((lasso_pred - y_test)^2)

# Baseline (just using the mean)
null_mse <- mean((mean(y_train) - y_test)^2)

# Compile results
results_df <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Null (Mean)",
            "Linear Regression",
            "Ridge Regression",
            "Lasso Regression"),
  Test_MSE = c(
    null_mse,
    linear_test_mse,
    ridge_test_mse,
    lasso_test_mse
  )
)
knitr::kable(results_df, caption = "Test Set Performance", digits = 2)

# Final Coefficient Table
coef_table <- data.frame(
  Variable = rownames(ridge_coef)[-1],
  Ridge = as.vector(ridge_coef[-1]),
  Lasso = as.vector(lasso_coef[-1])
)
knitr::kable(coef_table, caption = "Lasso Coefficients at Best Lambda", digits = 3)
```


Okay so overall for Lasso regression, Lasso did NOT shrink any coefficient to zero at the optimal lambda, which is 0.01. A larger lambda grid would be needed to do so.

Lasso test MSE is 1704.62, and the Null model MSE is 3335.12..... basically, our weather-based model significantly outperforms the predicted average!

Final observation, from all methods essentially: Temperature (TEMP), Wind Speed (WSPM), and Dew Point (DEWP) are the strongest positive drivers of O3, and Pressure (PRES) shows a negative effect, while Rain (RAIN) has a near-zero coefficient on Ozone.
